title: The Green Revolution

endcard.line: Pictures: Greenpenguin3459 (CC BY 4.0); unknown photographer (public domain)

segments.say: In nineteen fifty to fifty-one, India produced fifty-one million tonnes of food grains. By twenty twenty-one to twenty-two, it was over three hundred and fourteen million.
A turning point came in the mid nineteen sixties: the Green Revolution, a large rise in grain output from high-yielding seeds, mainly of wheat and rice.

items.text: dwarf rice and wheat seed imported
'Green Revolution' named; India issues a stamp

segments.say: From nineteen sixty-four, India imported seed of dwarf rice and wheat. In nineteen sixty-eight, the term Green Revolution was coined, and India marked it with a postage stamp.
The new seeds needed reliable water, fertiliser and pesticide. Farmers who could afford them gained the most.

left.title: Mid-1960s to mid-1970s
items: richer states: Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu

segments.say: At first, the gains stayed mostly with wheat and better-off states like Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. In the second phase, they spread to more states and crops.

anim.title: What it changed
items: A surplus for farmers to sell
Less reliance on other nations for food

segments.say: India became self-sufficient in food grains, and no longer had to depend on other nations to feed itself.
For GS One and GS Three, remember: high-yielding seeds, the mid nineteen sixties, wheat first, and gains that were uneven across regions.

sources: ICAR, 'Indian Agriculture after Independence' (2022, read): food grain production rose from 51 Mt in 1950-51 to over 314 Mt in 2021-22; the Green Revolution in the mid-1960s; the term coined by William Gaud of USAID in 1968, the same year India issued a commemorative postal stamp; 1966 introduction of IR8; imports of seed of dwarf varieties of rice and wheat from 1964 onwards

NCERT Class 11, Indian Economic Development, ch. 2 (keec102, read): the green revolution refers to the large increase in food grain production from HYV seeds, especially wheat and rice; HYV seeds needed reliable irrigation and money for fertiliser and pesticide; first phase (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) restricted to more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu and mainly wheat; second phase (mid-1970s to mid-1980s) spread to more states and crops; India achieved self-sufficiency in food grains; marketed surplus

quiz.q: In the first phase of the Green Revolution, which crop gained most?
quiz.why: NCERT: HYV seeds primarily benefited wheat-growing regions at first.

quiz.q: India's food grain production in 1950-51 was about…
quiz.why: ICAR: 51 Mt in 1950-51; over 314 Mt in 2021-22.

quiz.q: Which was NOT one of the states named for the first phase?
quiz.why: NCERT names Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
